documentNotes.statement:
**Indian National Physics Olympiad – 2018**

Date: **28 January 2018**. Time: **09:00–12:00 (3 hours)**. Maximum Marks: **75**.

Roll Number: $1\,8\,\square\,\square-\square\,\square\,\square\,\square-\square\,\square\,\square\,\square$.

I permit/do not permit (strike out one) HBCSE to reveal my academic performance and personal details to a third party.

Besides the International Physics Olympiad (IPhO) 2018, do you also want to be considered for the Asian Physics Olympiad (APhO) 2018? For APhO 2018 and its pre-departure training, your presence will be required in Delhi and Vietnam from April 28 to May 15, 2018. In principle, you can participate in both Olympiads. **Yes/No.**

Full Name (BLOCK letters) Ms./Mr.: [blank].

Extra sheets attached: [blank box]. Date: [blank]. Centre (e.g. Kochi): [blank]. Signature: [blank].

**(Do not write below this line)**

### Instructions

1. This booklet consists of 27 pages (excluding this sheet) and total of 7 questions.
2. This booklet is divided in two parts: **Questions with Summary Answer Sheet** and **Detailed Answer Sheet**. Write roll number at the top wherever asked.
3. The **final answer to each sub-question** should be **neatly written in the box provided below each sub-question** in the **Questions & Summary Answer Sheet**.
4. You are also required to show your detailed work for each question in a reasonably neat and coherent way in the **Detailed Answer Sheet**. You must write the relevant Question Number(s) on each of these pages.
5. Marks will be awarded on the basis of what you write on both the **Summary Answer Sheet** and the **Detailed Answer Sheet**. Simple short answers and plots may be directly entered in the **Summary Answer Sheet**. Marks may be deducted for absence of detailed work in questions involving longer calculations. Strike out any rough work that you do not want to be considered for evaluation.
6. Adequate space has been provided in the answersheet for you to write/calculate your answers. In case you need extra space to write, you may request additional blank sheets from the invigilator. Write your roll number on the extra sheets and get them attached to your answersheet and indicate number of extra sheets attached at the top of this page.
7. Non-programmable scientific calculators are allowed. Mobile phones cannot be used as calculators.
8. Use blue or black pen to write answers. Pencil may be used for diagrams/graphs/sketches.
9. This **entire booklet must be returned** at the end of the examination.

problems.title: The Yukawa potential
problems.statement:
In a nucleus, the attractive central potential which binds the proton and the neutron is called the Yukawa potential. The associated potential energy $U(r)$ is

$$U(r)=-\alpha\frac{e^{-r/\lambda}}r$$

Here $\lambda=1.431\ \mathrm{fm}$ ($\mathrm{fm}=10^{-15}\ \mathrm m$), $r$ is the distance between nucleons, and $\alpha=86.55\ \mathrm{MeV\cdot fm}$ is the nuclear force constant ($1\ \mathrm{MeV}=1.60\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm J$). Assume nuclear force constant $\alpha$ to be $A\hbar c$. Here $\hbar=h/2\pi$ and $h$ is Planck’s constant. In order to compare the nuclear force to other fundamental forces of nature within the nucleus of Deuterium ($\,{}^2\mathrm H$), let the constants associated with the electrostatic force and the gravitational force to be equal to $B\hbar c$ and $C\hbar c$ respectively. Here $A$, $B$ and $C$ are dimensionless. State the expression and numerical values of $A$, $B$ and $C$.

**Summary answer fields:** $A=$ [blank]; Value of $A=$ [blank]; $B=$ [blank]; Value of $B=$ [blank]; $C=$ [blank]; Value of $C=$ [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

**Native answer booklet:** PDF pages8–25 and28 (printed pages7–24 and27) are nineteen blank Detailed Answers pages with a “Que. No.” box and an alternate-page “Last four digits of Roll No.:” field. Every sheet remains in the complete original; the first complete blank template is retained here.

problems.title: The shadow of a sphere
problems.statement: An opaque sphere of radius $R$ lies on a horizontal plane. On the perpendicular through the point of contact, there is a point source of light at a distance $R$ above the top of the sphere (i.e. $3R$ from the plane).

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
Find the area of the shadow of the sphere on the plane.

**Summary answer field:** Area = [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
A transparent liquid of refractive index $\sqrt3$ is filled above the plane such that the sphere is just covered with liquid. Find the area of the shadow of the sphere on the plane now.

**Summary answer field:** Area = [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

solution.statement:
### (a)

[[figure:p2-key-shadow-air]]

MP is the radius $r$ of the shadow on ground. Let, $\angle\mathrm{MSP}=\theta$. Triangles OSQ and SMP are similar.

$$\frac{\mathrm{MP}}{\mathrm{MS}}=\frac{\mathrm{OQ}}{\mathrm{SQ}}$$

$$\Rightarrow\frac r{3R}=\frac R{\sqrt{\mathrm{OS}^2-\mathrm{OQ}^2}}=\frac R{\mathrm{SQ}}=\frac R{R\sqrt3}$$

$$r=R\sqrt3$$

Area of the shadow $=3\pi R^2$.

### (b)

[[figure:p2-key-shadow-liquid]]

Ray from $S$ is refracted at $N$. New radius of shadow is $\mathrm{MP'}=r'$. Also, $\angle\mathrm{N'NP'}=\theta$. In $\triangle\mathrm{NP'N'}$

$$\cos\theta=\frac{\mathrm{NN'}}{\mathrm{NP'}}=\frac{2R}{r'+R\tan i}$$

$$r'+R\tan i=\frac{2R}{\cos\theta}=2R\sec\theta$$

$$\begin{aligned}r'&=\mathrm{P'N'}+\mathrm{N'M}\\&=2R\tan\theta+R\tan i\end{aligned}$$

which yields

$$\sec\theta-\tan\theta=\tan i$$

$$\Rightarrow2i=\frac\pi2-\theta$$

$$\Rightarrow\sin\theta=\frac{\sin i}{\sqrt3}=\frac13$$

$$r'=2R\tan\theta+R\tan i=2R\frac1{\sqrt8}+R\frac1{\sqrt2}=R\sqrt2$$

Area of the shadow $=2\pi R^2$.

**Source note:** The native key prints the denominator $\mathrm{NP'}$ and $r'+R\tan i$ in the cosine equality, then $r'+R\tan i=2R\sec\theta$. These printed intermediate equalities do not agree with the later relations for $r'$, $\sec\theta-\tan\theta$ and the pictured geometry. All signs, symbols and the final answer remain as printed.

problems.title: An infinite ladder of resistors
problems.statement:
Consider an infinite ladder of resistors. The input current $I_0$ is indicated in the figure.

[[figure:p3-ladder]]

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
Find the equivalent resistance of the ladder.

**Summary answer field:** Equivalent resistance = [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
Find the recursion relation obeyed by the currents through the horizontal resistors $r$. You will get a relationship where $I_n$ will be related to (may be several) $I_i$s, $i<n$, $n>0$.

**Summary answer field:** Relation: [blank].

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:
Solve this for the special case $R=r$ to obtain $I_n$ and $I'_n$ as explicit functions of $n$. You may have to make a reasonable assumption about the behaviour of $I_n$ as $n$ becomes large.

**Summary answer fields:** $I_n=$ [blank]; $I'_n=$ [blank].

parts.label: d)
parts.statement:
If the ladder is chopped off after the $N$-th node (so that $I_{N+1}=0$) what will the form of $I_n/I_N$ be for $n\le N$?

**Summary answer field:** $I_n/I_N=$ [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

figures.alt: Complete original infinite resistor ladder, input I0, horizontal r, vertical R, In−1/In and primed branch currents, all ellipses.

solution.statement:
### (a)

[[figure:p3-key-equivalent]]

Let equivalent resistance be $X$

$$r+\frac{RX}{R+X}=X$$

$$X=\frac{r\pm\sqrt{r^2+4rR}}2$$

Taking positive sign

$$X=\frac{r+\sqrt{r^2+4rR}}2$$

### (b)

From Kirchhoff’s circuit law

$$I_{n-1}=I_n+I'_n\tag{1}$$

Using Kirchhoff’s voltage law

$$rI_n+RI'_{n+1}-RI'_n=0\tag{2}$$

From Eq. (1) we see that

$$I'_{n+1}-I'_n=(I_n-I_{n+1})-(I_{n-1}-I_n)=2I_n-I_{n+1}-I_{n-1}$$

So that Eq. (2) becomes

$$I_{n+1}-\left(2+\frac rR\right)I_n+I_{n-1}=0\tag{3}$$

which is the required recursion relation.

### (c)

**First method:**

One can see that $I_{n-1}$, $I_n$, $I_{n+1}$ form geometric progression. Also

[[figure:p3-key-geometric-circuits]]

$$I_1=I_0\frac R{R+X}\qquad\text{(see the figure to the left)}$$

$$I_2=I_1\frac R{R+X}=I_0\left(\frac R{R+X}\right)^2\qquad\text{(see the figure to the right)}$$

Hence

$$I_n=I_0\left(\frac R{R+X}\right)^n$$

For $r=R$,

$$I_n=I_0\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\right)^n=I_0k^n=I_0\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}2\right)^{2n}$$

Using Eq. (2)

$$I'_n=I_0\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}2\right)\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\right)^{n-1}=I_0\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}2\right)^{2n-1}$$

**Second method:**

For $R=r$, Eq. (3) becomes

$$I_{n+1}-3I_n+I_{n-1}=0\tag{4}$$

We can solve this linear recursion relation by assuming the ansatz $I_n\sim\rho^n$. This leads to

$$\rho^2-3\rho+1=0$$

so that we have

$$\rho=\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}2$$

This means that the general solution to (4) is

$$I_n=A\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\right)^n+B\left(\frac{3+\sqrt5}2\right)^n\tag{5}$$

The second term grows without bound with increasing $n$ - so that for an infinite ladder we must have $B=0$. Also when $n=0$, $I_0=A$. Thus

$$I_n=I_0\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\right)^n$$

$$I'_n=I_{n-1}-I_n=I_0\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}2\right)\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\right)^{n-1}$$

### (d)

**First method:** Consider the end part of the ladder as shown below.

[[figure:p3-key-end-currents]]

Voltage drop across AB $=2RI_N=I'_NR\Rightarrow I'_N=2I_N$ and $I_{N-1}=3I_N$.

Voltage drop across CD $=\frac{5R}3\,3I_N=I'_{N-1}R\Rightarrow I'_{N-1}=5I_N$ and $I_{N-2}=8I_N$.

Voltage drop across EF $=\frac{13R}8\,8I_N=I'_{N-2}R\Rightarrow I'_{N-2}=13I_N$ and $I_{N-3}=21I_N..$

This is depicted in figure below.

[[figure:p3-key-fibonacci-circuit]]

This looks like the terms of Fibonacci sequence. Fibonacci sequence is 1,1,2,3,5,8,13...etc in which $n$th term of Fibonacci sequence is the sum of previous two terms i.e. $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$, $F_1=F_2=1$. In other words:

$$I_{N-1}=F_4,\ I_{N-2}=F_6,\ I_{N-3}=F_8,\ I_{N-4}=F_{10}\ldots$$

In general

$$\frac{I_{N-r}}{I_N}=F_{2r+2}\tag{6}$$

$$\frac{I_n}{I_N}=F_{2(N-n)+2}\tag{7}$$

**Second method:** See Eq. 5. If $I_{N+1}=0$, we must have

$$A\rho_1^{N+1}+B\rho_2^{N+1}=0$$

where $\rho_{2,1}=(3\pm\sqrt5)/2$. Thus $B=-A(\rho_1/\rho_2)^{N+1}$ and thus

$$I_n=A\left(\rho_1^n-\rho_2^n\left(\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}\right)^{N+1}\right)$$

and thus

$$\frac{I_n}{I_N}=\frac{\rho_1^n-\rho_2^n(\rho_1/\rho_2)^{N+1}}{\rho_1^N-\rho_2^N(\rho_1/\rho_2)^{N+1}}=\frac{\rho_1\rho_2}{\rho_2-\rho_1}\left[\rho_1^{n-N-1}-\rho_2^{n-N-1}\right]$$

Substituting the values, we get

$$\frac{I_n}{I_N}=\frac1{\sqrt5}\left[\left(\frac{3+\sqrt5}2\right)^{N+1-n}-\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\right)^{N+1-n}\right]\tag{8}$$

Equations (7) and (8) are equivalent.

**Generalization**

if $r\ne R$:

Solution to Eq. (3) is

$$\rho_{2,1}=\frac{b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4}}2\quad\text{where}\quad b=2+\frac rR$$

Thus

$$\frac{I_n}{I_N}=\frac{\rho_1\rho_2}{\rho_2-\rho_1}\left[\rho_1^{n-N-1}-\rho_2^{n-N-1}\right]\tag{9}$$

$$=\frac1{\rho_2-\rho_1}\left[\rho_2^{N+1-n}-\rho_1^{N+1-n}\right]\tag{10}$$

Alternate form of Eqs. (7), (8) and (10) are also accepted.

**Source note:** Before Eq. (6), the source equates the currents $I_{N-1},I_{N-2},\ldots$ directly to dimensionless Fibonacci terms without an $I_N$ factor. The subsequent equations explicitly use current ratios. Both printed forms are retained.

problems.title: An hour glass on a weighing scale
problems.statement:
An hour glass is placed on a weighing scale. Initially all the sand of mass $m_0$ kg in the glass is held in the upper reservoir (ABC) and the mass of the glass alone is $M$ kg. At $t=0$, the sand is released. It exits the upper reservoir at constant rate $dm/dt=\lambda$ kg/s where $m$ is the mass of the sand in the upper reservoir at time $t$ sec. Assume that the speed of the falling sand is zero at the neck of the glass and after it falls through a constant height $h$ it instantaneously comes to rest on the floor (DE) of the hour glass. Obtain the reading on the scale for all times $t>0$. Make a detailed plot of the reading vs time.

[[figure:p4-hourglass]]

**Summary answer field:** Reading on the scale: [blank].

[[figure:p4-blank-plot]]

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

figures.alt: Whole native hourglass and weighing scale, upper ABC, lower DE, constant h arrow and dial.
Complete blank Reading (kg) versus time frame, both axes, arrows and labels.

solution.statement:
Velocity of grain when reaches to bottom $v=\sqrt{2gh}$. At $t=0$, sand is released. Time taken $t_1=\sqrt{2h/g}$.

### $0<t<t_1$

For $t<0$, the scale was $(m+M)g$. As $t=0\to t_1$, more sand will enter the mid air portion and hence the reading will drop,

$$\lambda=\frac{dm}{dt}\Rightarrow m=\lambda t\tag{11}$$

$$\text{Weight }(W_1)=(M+m)g-\lambda t_1g\tag{12}$$

### $t_1<t<t_2$

Here $t_2=m/\lambda$ is the time when all the sand has left the upper reservoir. Just after $t=t_1$, force on the scale will partly due to weight of sand as given in above equation and partly due to impulse provided by falling sand.

$$\text{Impulse force}=v\frac{dm}{dt}=\lambda\sqrt{2gh}\tag{13}$$

$$\text{Weight }(W_2)=[(M=m)g-\lambda t_1g]+\lambda\sqrt{2gh}=(M+m)g\tag{14}$$

### $t_2<t<t_3$

Here $t_3=m/\lambda+\sqrt{2h/g}$. This is the time span between the sand has left upper reservoir to when all sand has reached the floor of the hour glass. The weight is

$$W_3=W_2+\lambda(t-t_2)g\tag{15}$$

### For $t>t_3$

weight is

$$W_4=(M+m)g$$

[[figure:p4-key-reading]]

**Source note:** These are literal printed key expressions. The question defines $m$ as the remaining mass in the upper reservoir but gives $dm/dt=+\lambda$; the key reuses $m$ both for flowing mass ($m=\lambda t$) and in total-weight/time expressions instead of the initial $m_0$. Eq. (12) prints $t_1$ although the native graph depicts a reading that decreases throughout the first interval. Eq. (14) prints an equals sign in $(M=m)$, while its final expression uses $(M+m)$. The graph assumes the pictured order $t_1<t_2<t_3$; the source does not supply a separate case for an upper reservoir that empties before the first grain arrives. No replacement formula or additional unprinted case has been inserted.

figures.alt: Full native scale-reading graph, three vertical levels m+M±λ√(2h/g), t1/t2/t3, discontinuities, origin, axis arrows and units.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
Consider two short identical magnets each of mass $M$ and each of which maybe considered as point dipoles of magnetic moment $\vec\mu$. One of them is fixed to the floor with its magnetic moment pointing upwards and the other one is free and found to float in equilibrium at a height $z$ above the fixed dipole. The magnetic field due to a point dipole at a distance $r$ from it is

$$\vec B(\vec r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^3}\left(3(\vec\mu\cdot\hat r)\hat r-\vec\mu\right)$$

Obtain an expression for the magnitude of the dipole moment of the magnet in terms of $z$ and related quantities.

**Summary answer field:** $\vec\mu=$ [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
**i. [1½ marks]** Consider a ring of mass $M_r$ rotating with uniform angular speed about its axis. A charge $q$ is smeared uniformly over it. Relate its angular momentum $\vec S_r$ to its magnetic moment ($\vec\mu_r$).

**Summary answer field:** $\vec\mu_r=$ [blank].

**ii. [1 mark]** Assume that the electron is a sphere of uniform charge density rotating about its diameter with constant angular speed. Also assume that the same relation as in the previous part holds between its angular momentum $\vec S$ and its magnetic dipole moment ($\vec\mu_B$). Further assume that $S=h/(2\pi)$ where $h$ is Planck’s constant. Calculate $\mu_B$.

**Summary answer field:** $\mu_B=$ [blank].

**iii. [3 marks]** Assume that the sole contribution to the dipole moment of a $\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}$ molecule comes from an unpaired electron. Also assume that the magnets in the part (5a) are $0.482\ \mathrm{kg}$ each of $\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}$ and the unpaired electrons of the molecules are all aligned. Calculate the height $z$. (Note: The molecular weight of $\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}=211$)

**Summary answer field:** $z=$ [blank].

**iv. [1½ marks]** In an experiment $\mu_B$ is aligned along a magnetic field of $1\ \mathrm T$. It is flipped in a direction anti-parallel to the magnetic field by an incident photon. What should be the wavelength of this photon?

**Summary answer field:** Wavelength = [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

solution.statement:
### (a)

Given

$$\vec B(\vec r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^3}\left[3(\vec\mu\cdot\hat r)\hat r-\vec\mu\right]$$

$$\hat r=\hat k,\quad r=z$$

$$\begin{aligned}\vec B(z)&=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi z^3}[3\mu\hat k-\mu\hat k]\\&=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi z^3}[2\mu\hat k]\end{aligned}$$

$$B(z)=\frac{\mu_0\mu}{2\pi z^3}$$

The magnets are oppositely facing along $\hat z$. The force on the upper magnet due to the lower fixed magnet is

$$\vec F=\frac{3\mu_0\mu^2}{2\pi z^4}$$

The repulsive magnetic force is balanced by the weight acting down.

$$Mg=\frac32\frac{\mu_0}{\pi z^4}\mu^2\tag{16}$$

$$\mu^2=\frac23\frac{\pi z^4}{\mu_0}Mg$$

$$\mu=\left(\frac{Mg\,4\pi}{6\mu_0}\right)^{1/2}z^2\tag{17}$$

### (b) i.

Let radius of the ring to be $R$ and it is rotating with the angular speed $\omega\hat z$. Dipole moment can be expressed as

$$\vec\mu_r=\text{current}\times\text{area}=\frac{q\omega}{2\pi}\pi R^2\hat z$$

$$\vec S_r=M_r\omega R^2\hat z$$

$$\Rightarrow\vec\mu_r=\frac q{2M_r}\vec S_r$$

### (b) ii.

$$\mu_B=\frac{e\hbar}{2m_e}=9.20\times10^{-24}\ \text{to}\ 9.30\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\cdot m^2}$$

### (b) iii.

The system (dipole) is made of $\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}$ and has one electron/molecule. The number of molecules is

$$=\frac{\text{Mass of }\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}\text{ in gm}}{\text{Molecular weight of }\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}}\times N_A\tag{18}$$

$$=\frac MA\times N_A\tag{19}$$

Assuming that each molecule of $\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}$ has one unpaired electron and each contributes to dipole moment. Further all of them are perfectly aligned. Hence dipole moment is

$$\mu=\frac{MN_A\mu_B}A\tag{20}$$

Using Eq. (17)

$$6.60\le z\ (\mathrm{cm})\le6.80$$

### (b) iv.

$$\text{Wavelength}=\frac{hc}{2\mu_BB}=1.00\ \text{to}\ 1.10\ \mathrm{cm}\tag{21}$$

**Source note:** The key writes a vector $\vec F$ equal to a scalar magnitude, and in Eq. (19) uses $M$ for mass in grams and $A$ for molecular weight without separately defining $A$; the question gives the magnet mass in kilograms. The preceding “in gm” wording, formulas and accepted ranges are preserved.

problems.title: The Van der Waals Gas
problems.statement:
Consider $n$ mole of a non-ideal (realistic) gas. Its equation of state maybe described by the Van der Waals equation

$$\left(P+\frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)\left(\frac Vn-b\right)=RT$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. We take one mole of the gas ($n=1$). You must bear in mind that one is often required to make judicious approximations to understand realistic systems.

sections.title: (a)
sections.statement: For this part only take $a=0$. Obtain expressions in terms of $V$, $T$ and constants for

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
the coefficient of volume expansion ($\beta$);

**Summary answer field:** $\beta=$ [blank].

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement:
the isothermal compressibility ($\kappa$).

**Summary answer field:** $\kappa=$ [blank].

sections.title: (b) Criticality
sections.statement:
The Van der Waals gas exhibits phase transition. A typical isotherm at low temperature is shown in the figure. Here $L$ ($G$) represents the liquid (gas) phase and at $P_{LG}$ there are three possible solutions for the volume ($V_L$, $V_{LG}$, $V_G$). As the temperature is raised, at a certain temperature $T_c$, the three values of the volume merge to a single value, $V_c$ (corresponding pressure being $P_c$). This is called the point of criticality. As the temperature is raised further there exists only one real solution for the volume and the isotherm resembles that of an ideal gas.

[[figure:p6-isotherms]]

solution.statement:
### (a) i.

$$\beta=\frac1V\left(\frac{dV}{dT}\right)_p=\frac{V-b}{VT}\tag{22}$$

### (a) ii.

$$\kappa=-\frac1V\left(\frac{dV}{dP}\right)_T=\frac{(V-b)^2}{VRT}\tag{23}$$

### (b) i.

At criticality, the curve is a cubic like function. Hence

$$\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_T=\left(\frac{d^2P}{dV^2}\right)_T=0$$

Above condition along with Van der Waal’s equation can be used to obtain

$$V_C=3b\tag{24}$$

$$T_C=\frac{8a}{27Rb}\tag{25}$$

$$P_C=\frac a{27b^2}\tag{26}$$

### (b) ii.

$a=0.37\ \mathrm{m^6\cdot Pa/mol^2}$ and $b=4.33\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3/mol}$.

### (b) iii.

$$b=N_Ad^3\quad\text{or}\quad N_A4\pi r^3/3$$

$$d=1.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm m\ \text{to}\ 6.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm m$$

### (c) i.

$$P_0V_G^2-RTV_G+a=0$$

$$V_G=\frac{RT}{2P_0}\left(1\pm\left(1-\frac{4aP_0}{R^2T^2}\right)^{1/2}\right)$$

Taking positive sign since in the ideal gas limit $a\longrightarrow0$, $V_I=RT/P_0$ for one mole.

$$V_G\simeq\frac{RT}{P_0}-\frac a{RT}$$

### (c) ii.

$$V_I=\frac{RT}{P_0}$$

### (c) iii.

Comment 1: For ideal gas, $a/RT$ vanishes as $T\to\infty$.

$$\frac{V_G-V_I}{V_I}=\frac{-aP_0}{(RT)^2}\simeq-5.50\times10^{-3}\ \text{to}\ -7.00\times10^{-3}$$

Comment 2: Answer is negative, indicating attractive intermolecular forces.

### (d) i.

In this phase $P\ll a/V_L^2$. Hence

$$\frac a{V_L^2}(V_L-b)=RT$$

$$V_L=\frac a{2RT}\left(1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{4bRT}a}\right)$$

Taking negative sign since as $T\to0$, $V_L\to b$.

$$\begin{aligned}V_L&=\frac a{2RT}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{4bRT}a}\right)\\&\simeq b\left(1+\frac{bRT}a\right)\end{aligned}$$

### (d) ii.

$$\rho_w\approx\frac{1.80\times10^{-2}}b=3.60\times10^2\ \text{to}\ 6.00\times10^2\ \mathrm{Kg/m^3}\tag{27}$$

### (d) iii.

$$L\times\text{molar mass}=\int_{V_L}^{V_G}\frac a{V^2}\,dV\simeq\frac a{V_L}$$

$$L\simeq6.0\times10^5\ \text{to}\ 1.1\times10^6\ \mathrm{J/Kg}$$

**Source note:** The density and heat-of-vaporization expressions are the approximations printed in the key. Its accepted ranges are retained in full; the source prints capital “Kg” in the two unit labels and upper-case critical subscripts $C$ in Eqs. (24)–(26).

problems.title: Water level in an inverted cylinder
problems.statement:
A small circular hole of diameter $d$ is punched on the side and the near the bottom of a transparent cylinder of diameter $D$. The hole is initially sealed and the cylinder is filled with water of density $\rho_w$. It is then inverted onto a bucket filled to the brim with water. The seal is removed, air rushes in and height $h(t)$ of the water level (as measured from the surface level of the water in the bucket) is recorded at different times ($t$). The figure below and the table in part (c) illustrates this process. Assume that air is an incompressible fluid with density $\rho_a$ and its motion into the cylinder is a streamline flow. Thus its speed $v$ is related to the pressure difference $\Delta P$ by the Bernoulli relation. Take the outside pressure $P_0$ to be atmospheric pressure $=1.00\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

solution.statement:
### (a)

at time $t$ from pressure balance equation

$$P_0=p+h\rho_wg$$

$$\Delta P=P_0-p=h\rho_wg$$

From Bernoulli’s principle

$$\frac12v^2\rho_a=h\rho_wg=\Delta P$$

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2\rho_wg}{\rho_a}}\sqrt h$$

The speed of air gushing in through the small hole is related to speed $v_w$ of fall of water level by

$$\frac{\pi d^2}4v=\frac{\pi D^2}4v_w\tag{28}$$

$$v_w=\frac{d^2}{D^2}\sqrt{\frac{2\rho_wg}{\rho_a}}\sqrt h\tag{29}$$

### (b)

$$v_w=-\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{d^2}{D^2}\sqrt{\frac{2\rho_wg}{\rho_a}}\sqrt h$$

$$\sqrt h=\sqrt{h_0}-\frac{d^2}{D^2}\sqrt{\frac{\rho_wg}{2\rho_a}}\,t$$

### (c)

The appended original handwritten graph sheet is retained in full.

[[figure:p7-key-handwritten-graph]]

**Native handwritten annotations:** The horizontal axis is $t$ (in sec), the vertical values are in $\sqrt{\mathrm{cm}}$, the marked origin is $(0,3.25)$, and the intercept is $4.78$. The vertical handwritten label uses $\sqrt{h_0}$ even though the plotted values vary with $t$.

Scale: On Xaxis $\to1\ \mathrm{cm}=0.33\ \mathrm{sec}$; Yaxis $\to1\ \mathrm{cm}=0.062\sqrt{\mathrm{cm}}$.

Marked coordinates: $(1.48,4.40)$ and $(4.42,3.63)$.

$$\text{Slope}=\frac{4.40-3.63}{1.48-4.42}=-2.61\times10^{-1}\ \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{cm}}}{\mathrm{sec}}$$

$$\Rightarrow\sqrt{h_0}=4.78$$

$$h_0=22.85\ \mathrm{cm}$$

### (d) i.

$$22.0\le h_0\ (\mathrm{cm})\le24.0$$

### (d) ii.

$$-0.27\le\text{slope}\ (\sqrt{\mathrm{cm}}/\mathrm s)\le-0.25$$

$$0.13\le d\ (\mathrm{cm})\le0.14$$

### (d) iii.

$$2.35\le v_w\ (\mathrm{cm/s})\le2.65$$

It contains the eight plotted data points, fit, construction lines, marked coordinates, units, scales, intercept and height calculation. The whole sheet remains available, including its printed header and the original handwritten $\sqrt{h_0}$ vertical label.
